passage: Note, Thursday. I look after Rafiq after school, and yesterday I watched him do something new. He asked his parents for ten minutes, sat them down and read from a paper: "If I may have a puppy, I will take it on the morning walk every day before school, and I will keep my marks at least where they were last term." His mother asked who would clean up. Rafiq said, "Me, and I will ask for help at first." His father smiled and called the offer fair, and they said they would think until Sunday. Rafiq nodded quickly, though his knee kept bouncing under the table. I told him waiting is part of the deal. Pooja

qa.q: What two things did Rafiq promise in return for a puppy?
qa.a: He promised to take it on the morning walk every day before school and to keep his marks at least where they were last term.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while he waited for his parents' answer?
qa.a: Nervous and hopeful, since his knee kept bouncing under the table even though he nodded quickly.

qa.q: What could Rafiq add to his offer if his parents remain unsure?
qa.a: He could suggest a trial period or offer some pocket money for supplies, because it lowers the risk for his parents.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's parents see the proposal compared with a plain "please"?
qa.a: It gives them something concrete to weigh, and his father called it fair, so they seem to see a child ready to take responsibility.

grounding: A boy offers his parents a deal, morning walks and steady marks, in exchange for a pet.

passage:
Saturday
Tonight I made my offer. I didn't beg this time. I wrote it on a sheet like a real deal: If we get a dog, 1) I, Darshan, will take him for the morning walk before school, every day, even in the rain. 2) My marks will stay at least where they are now. 3) If I miss the walk three times in a month, we talk again. Gautam-bhaiya said number 3 was clever because it shows I'm serious. Papa read it twice. Mummy asked, "Who walks him when you have a school trip?" I hadn't thought of that. Bhaiya said he'd do those days. Papa said they'd think about it for a week. A week is not a no!
Darshan

qa.q: What does Darshan promise to do before school?
qa.a: Take the dog for the morning walk every day, even in the rain.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel about Papa's answer?
qa.a: Hopeful, even excited, since 'a week is not a no'.

qa.q: What else could Darshan add to the offer?
qa.a: A plan for other gaps, like feeding when the family is away, worked out with Papa and Mummy.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the deal?
qa.a: Mummy seems to take it seriously, since she looks for gaps like school trips rather than refusing.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child offering a clear exchange, walks and steady marks, in return for having a dog.

passage: In their village near Sangli, a stray puppy had followed Darshan home along the school path three days running. On the fourth day he didn't beg Aai to keep it. He waited until she was sorting rice on the verandah and sat beside her with his school diary. "Aai, if we keep her, I'll walk her to the fields and back every morning before school. And my marks won't drop. You can check my diary every Friday." His sister Pooja added, "I'll feed her when he has cricket." Aai kept sorting. "And if your marks drop?" "Then she goes to live with Pooja's friend's family," Darshan said, swallowing hard. Aai looked at the puppy, then at him. "One month. Show me."

qa.q: When did Darshan sit beside Aai?
qa.a: While she was sorting rice on the verandah.

qa.q: What does Darshan swallowing hard suggest?
qa.a: He felt nervous; the consequence was hard to say, but he wanted to show he was serious.

qa.q: What else could Darshan offer Aai?
qa.a: A weekly check with her on the walks as well as the marks, so she sees the whole deal working.

qa.q: How does Aai see the deal?
qa.a: Aai takes it seriously and gives a one-month trial to see if Darshan keeps it.

grounding: A boy offers daily walks and steady marks in exchange for keeping a puppy, giving his mother a fair deal to try.
